fig1_submerged_fraction.svg: For a freely floating body the buoyant force equals the weight, and the submerged fraction reduces to the density ratio $\rho_{body}/\rho_{fluid}$ (submerged_fraction). Ice at 917 kg/m$^3$ therefore floats with 92% of its volume under water — the iceberg rule — while cork shows three-quarters of itself above the surface. At a ratio of 1 the line reaches full submersion and the body is neutrally buoyant; beyond it (floats $\rightarrow$ False) there is no equilibrium and it sinks.
fig2_apparent_weight.svg: A 10 L steel block weighs 0.77 kN in vacuum. Immersed, the fluid pushes back with $F_b=\rho_f gV$ (buoyant_force) and the scale reads the difference (apparent_weight) — a straight line falling with fluid density. Water removes only 0.10 kN, about 13% of the weight; the reading reaches zero exactly when the fluid density matches the block's own, and a denser fluid than that would float it. This is the fluid-statics leaf of the map — the mechanics trunk (CM) develops it further.
